Main functionGrowth, repairVariability + reductionSeparate chromatids
4.3.4 Mitotic and meiotic cell divisions in the eukaryotic life cycle
  • Meiosis forms haploid gametes in sexually reproducing organisms.
  • Fertilization unites two gametes and restores the diploid number.
  • From the zygote, mitosis enables growth, development and formation of the multicellular organism.
  • In the eukaryotic life cycle, meiosis, fertilization and mitosis complement each other.
  • Key: meiosis reduces chromosomes; fertilization restores them; mitosis maintains the chromosome number in somatic cells.
4.4.1 Physical basis of inheritance: basic concepts
  • Gene: unit of hereditary information.
  • Allele: alternative version of a gene.
  • Locus: position occupied by a gene on a chromosome.
  • Genotype: genetic composition of an individual; phenotype: observable expression.
  • Homozygous: two identical alleles; heterozygous: two different alleles.
  • Key: do not confuse genotype with phenotype; phenotype results from the expression of the genotype and its interaction with the environment.
4.4.1.1 Mendelian inheritance: general idea
  • Mendelian inheritance explains how certain traits are transmitted from one generation to the next through alleles.
  • It is based on segregation of alleles during gamete formation and on the combination of those alleles during fertilization.
  • Its principles work best for traits determined by a single gene with simple dominance.
  • Key: Mendelian inheritance connects the basic concepts of gene, allele and genotype with the proportions observed in offspring.
  • Mistake: not all hereditary traits follow simple Mendelian patterns.
4.4.2 Mendel's Laws
  • Law of segregation: the two alleles of a pair separate during gamete formation.
  • Law of independent assortment: genes on different chromosomes are distributed independently.
  • Punnett squares allow prediction of expected genotypes and phenotypes in offspring.
  • In an independent dihybrid cross, the classic F2 phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1.
  • The test cross helps infer the genotype of an individual with a dominant phenotype.
  • Worked example — monohybrid cross Aa × Aa: Let A = dominant (e.g. tall stem), a = recessive (e.g. short stem). Each parent produces gametes A and a in equal proportion. The Punnett square gives: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa (genotypic ratio 1:2:1). Phenotypically: 3 tall (AA + Aa) : 1 short (aa) → phenotypic ratio 3:1. Frequency of heterozygote Aa = 2/4 = 50 %. Mistake: confusing 1:2:1 (genotype) with 3:1 (phenotype); they are different ratios.
  • Worked example — dihybrid cross AaBb × AaBb: With independent assortment, you get 9 combinations with at least one dominant A and one dominant B : 3 dominant A, homozygous b : 3 homozygous a, dominant B : 1 aabb → phenotypic ratio 9:3:3:1. This ratio is a key exam answer.
  • Calculation: may require Punnett squares, probabilities, mono- and dihybrid ratios.
  • Mistake: Mendelian independence does not apply the same way when there is genetic linkage.
4.4.7 Non-Mendelian patterns
  • Incomplete dominance: heterozygote with intermediate phenotype.
  • Codominance: both alleles expressed (e.g. type AB).
  • ABO: 3 alleles IA, IB, i → 6 genotypes.
  • Polygenic inheritance: multiple genes → continuous trait (height, skin color).
  • Pleiotropy: one gene → multiple phenotypic effects.
4.4.8 Epigenetics
  • Epigenetics studies heritable changes in gene expression without modifying the DNA base sequence.
  • It can involve DNA methylation and histone modifications.
  • These mechanisms activate or silence genes according to cell type, developmental stage or environment.
  • It helps explain why cells with the same DNA can have different functions.
  • Mistake: epigenetics does not mean mutation; the DNA sequence can remain unchanged.
4.4.9 Genetic linkage
  • Genes located on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together.
  • The closer two genes are, the less likely they are to be separated by crossing over.
  • Crossing over can break linkage and generate recombination.
  • Linkage modifies the expected proportions when compared to Mendelian independence.
  • Calculation: may relate to proportions of recombinants and non-recombinants if the course requires it.
  • Mistake: do not assume gene independence just because two traits are being studied.
4.4.10 Sex-linked inheritance and human genetic disorders
  • Some hereditary disorders result from gene mutations and others from chromosomal abnormalities.
  • Sex-linked inheritance refers to genes located on the sex chromosomes, especially on the X chromosome.
  • In males (XY), a recessive allele on the X chromosome is more likely to be expressed because there is no second X chromosome allele to mask it.
  • Examples of X-linked recessive traits are hemophilia and color blindness, which is why they are more frequently observed in males.
  • In contrast, Down, Turner and Klinefelter syndromes are examples of chromosomal abnormalities, not X-linked recessive inheritance.
  • Down corresponds to trisomy 21, Turner to X0 and Klinefelter to XXY.
  • Nondisjunction during meiosis can give rise to gametes with an abnormal chromosome number.
  • Calculation: may require sex-linked inheritance crosses or inference of family probabilities.
  • Mistake: do not confuse a disorder caused by a sex-linked gene mutation with an abnormality in chromosome number.
4.4.11 Reading pedigrees (family trees)
  • A pedigree is a family diagram used to trace how a trait is inherited. Square = male, circle = female, filled symbol = affected, horizontal line between two = mating, vertical line = offspring.
  • How to identify the inheritance pattern:
  • → Recessive: the trait can "skip" generations; two UNaffected parents can have an affected child (both were heterozygous carriers).
  • → Dominant: the trait appears in every generation; each affected individual has at least one affected parent.
  • → Autosomal: affects males and females equally.
  • → X-linked recessive: affects males far more; an affected male does NOT pass it to his sons (he gives them the Y), but ALL his daughters become carriers.
  • Exam strategy: ①Does it skip generations? → recessive. ②Does it affect more males? → suspect X-linked. ③Assign genotypes starting from the affected individuals (recessives = homozygous) and work backward.
  • 🔬 Scenario: two parents with normal vision have a color-blind son. Genotypes? The mother must be a carrier (XᴰXᵈ) and the father normal (XᴰY); the affected son is XᵈY and received the Xᵈ from his mother.
  • Mistake: assuming a trait more common in males is Y-linked; it is almost always X-linked recessive.
4.5 DNA: structure and replication
  • Structure: nucleotide = phosphate group + deoxyribose + base (A, T, G, C). Antiparallel double helix. Base pairing via H-bonds: A=T (2 bonds) and G≡C (3 bonds, stronger). Chargaff's rules: %A=%T and %G=%C. Watson and Crick model (1953), X-ray diffraction data from Franklin.
  • Semiconservative replication: each daughter molecule retains one old strand + one new strand. Demonstrated by Meselson and Stahl (1958) with nitrogen isotopes.
  • Bidirectional replication: starts at replication origins (one in prokaryotes, many in eukaryotes) and proceeds as two forks in opposite directions.
  • Key enzymes (order at the fork):
  • → Helicase: opens the double helix by breaking H-bonds.
  • → Topoisomerase (gyrase in prokaryotes): relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork. Many antibiotics (quinolones) target bacterial gyrase.
  • → SSB: keep single strands separated and protect them.
  • → Primase: synthesizes the RNA primer (~10 nt). DNA polymerase cannot start from scratch: it needs a free 3'-OH end.
  • → DNA pol III (prok.) / Pol δ and ε (euk.): synthesizes new DNA in the 5'→3' direction, reads the template strand 3'→5'. Has proofreading activity.
  • → DNA pol I: removes RNA primers and fills gaps with DNA.
  • → DNA ligase: seals nicks by joining Okazaki fragments.
  • → Telomerase: extends telomeres to prevent progressive shortening of the lagging strand.
  • Leading strand (continuous): synthesized in a single continuous step toward the fork. One primer.
  • Lagging strand (discontinuous): synthesized in Okazaki fragments (away from the fork) because the polymerase can only synthesize 5'→3' and the template strand runs in the opposite direction.
  • ✏️ Fill in: The enzyme ___ (helicase) opens the double helix. ___ (topoisomerase) relieves supercoiling. ___ (SSB) proteins prevent strand reannealing. ___ (primase) synthesizes the primer. DNA polymerase synthesizes in the ___ (5'→3') direction. On the lagging strand, ___ (Okazaki) fragments form, joined by ___ (DNA ligase). ___ (telomerase) extends the telomeres.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if topoisomerase fails? DNA ahead of the fork would accumulate so much torsional stress from supercoiling that helicase could not advance and replication would stop. (Application: antibiotics such as ciprofloxacin inhibit bacterial gyrase.)
  • 🔬 Scenario: Why is the lagging strand synthesized in Okazaki fragments? Because DNA polymerase only synthesizes 5'→3', and the lagging template strand runs in the direction opposite to fork movement; it is therefore synthesized in short fragments "backward".
  • ⚠️ Mistake: DNA polymerase NEVER synthesizes 3'→5'. It only adds nucleotides to the 3'-OH end. That is why it needs a primer and why the lagging strand exists.
Enzyme / proteinFunction
HelicaseBreaks hydrogen bonds and opens the double helix
Topoisomerase (gyrase)Relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork. Target of quinolone antibiotics
SSBKeeps single strands separated and protects them from nucleases
PrimaseSynthesizes the RNA primer (~10 nt); DNA pol cannot start from scratch
DNA polymerase III / Pol δ and εSynthesizes new DNA in the 5'→3' direction; has proofreading activity
DNA polymerase IRemoves RNA primers and fills gaps with DNA
DNA ligaseSeals nicks by joining Okazaki fragments
TelomeraseExtends telomeres; active in germline cells and cancers
4.5.1 DNA as genetic material
  • DNA stores hereditary information in most organisms.
  • Its stable structure and capacity for replication allow information to be transmitted from one generation to the next.
  • Genes are segments of DNA that contain functional information.
  • DNA directs the synthesis of RNA and proteins through gene expression.
  • Key: DNA as genetic material implies storage, transmission and expression of information.
4.5.4 Mutations
  • Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence. Origin: spontaneous (replication errors) or induced (UV radiation, X-rays, chemical mutagens).
  • Gene mutations by mechanism — substitution: one base is replaced by another. Transition: purine↔purine or pyrimidine↔pyrimidine (A↔G, C↔T). Transversion: purine↔pyrimidine (A↔C, G↔T).
  • Insertion: one or more bases are added → shifts the reading frame. Gene deletion: one or more bases are lost → also shifts the reading frame.
  • Gene mutations by effect on the protein:
  • → Silent: changes the codon but does NOT change the amino acid (thanks to code degeneracy). Usually occurs at the 3rd base of the codon.
  • → Missense: changes the codon AND changes the amino acid. Classic example: GAG→GUG in β-globin changes glutamic acid to valine → sickle cell anemia.
  • → Nonsense: introduces a premature stop codon → truncated protein, generally non-functional.
  • → Frameshift: insertion or deletion of bases (not a multiple of 3) that shifts the reading frame → changes all codons downstream of the mutation point → completely different protein from that point on.
  • Structural chromosomal mutations: Deletion: loss of a fragment (e.g. Cri-du-chat syndrome from deletion of the short arm of chr. 5). Duplication: fragment appears twice. Inversion: fragment is inverted. Translocation: fragment moves to another chromosome (e.g. 9-22 translocation → Philadelphia chromosome → chronic myeloid leukemia).
  • ✏️ Fill in: Loss of a chromosomal fragment is called ___ (deletion), its double appearance is ___ (duplication), inverted is ___ (inversion), and moved to another chromosome is ___ (translocation). A substitution that does not change the amino acid is ___ (silent). One that introduces a premature stop codon is ___ (nonsense). An insertion/deletion that shifts the reading frame is ___ (frameshift).
  • Key: mutation is the original source of new alleles. Without mutation there is no variation; without variation there is no evolution.
  • ⚠️ Mistake: mutation does not always mean serious disease. A silent mutation does not change the protein. The effect depends on the type of change and its context.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if a mutation introduces a stop codon in the middle of a gene? Translation terminates early → truncated protein, generally non-functional (nonsense mutation). It can cause serious disease if the protein is essential.
4.6 Gene expression and regulation
  • DNA → mRNA (transcription, in nucleus) → protein (translation, ribosome).
  • AUG = start; UAA/UAG/UGA = stop. Codon = triplet in mRNA.
  • Eukaryotes: introns removed, exons joined; poly-A tail and 5' cap.
  • lac operon = regulation in prokaryotes.
4.6.1 The genetic code
  • The genetic code maps mRNA codons to specific amino acids.
  • It is nearly universal, degenerate and unambiguous.
  • Degenerate: different codons can encode the same amino acid.
  • Unambiguous: each codon specifies only one amino acid or signal.
  • Mistake: a codon is not the same as a gene; a codon is a triplet, not a complete protein.
4.6.2 Transcription
  • Transcription copies information from DNA to an RNA molecule. In eukaryotes it occurs in the nucleus.
  • Eukaryotic RNA polymerases: RNA Pol I transcribes ribosomal RNA. RNA Pol II transcribes mRNA (protein-coding genes). RNA Pol III transcribes tRNA and small RNAs.
  • TATA box: promoter sequence located ~25–30 nt before the transcription start site. It serves as an anchor for transcription factors that recruit RNA Pol II.
  • Transcription factors: proteins that bind the promoter and help (or prevent) transcription of specific genes. They are the basis of differential gene regulation.
  • Pre-mRNA processing in eukaryotes: ①Addition of 5' cap (7-methylguanosine; protects against degradation and facilitates translation initiation). ②3' polyadenylation (poly-A tail, ~200 A; stabilizes the mRNA). ③Splicing: removal of introns and joining of exons by the spliceosome.
  • Alternative splicing: exons from the same pre-mRNA can be combined in different ways → a single gene can produce several different proteins.
  • ⚠️ Mistake: do not confuse the template strand (3'→5', read by the polymerase) with the coding strand (5'→3', same sequence as the mRNA with U instead of T).
  • ✏️ Fill in: The RNA pol that transcribes protein-coding genes is ___ (RNA Pol II). The promoter site where it binds is called the ___ (TATA box). The process by which introns are removed is called ___ (splicing), carried out by the ___ (spliceosome) complex. The protection of the 5' end of the mRNA is called the ___ (5' cap).
4.6.3 Translation (expanded)
  • Types of RNA: mRNA (carries the message), tRNA (transports amino acids; recognizes codons through its anticodon), rRNA (structural and catalytic component of the ribosome — it is a ribozyme).
  • Ribosome in prokaryotes: 30S + 50S = 70S. In eukaryotes: 40S + 60S = 80S.
  • Ribosome sites: A site (aminoacyl: incoming charged tRNA). P site (peptidyl: growing chain; peptide bond forms here). E site (exit: empty tRNA leaves).
  • Initiation: in prokaryotes, the small subunit recognizes the Shine-Dalgarno sequence near the AUG. In eukaryotes, it recognizes the 5' cap and scans to the AUG in a Kozak context.
  • Elongation: aminoacyl-tRNA enters the A site → peptidyl transferase catalyzes the peptide bond → translocation: the ribosome advances one codon → the tRNA moves A→P→E.
  • Termination: a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) reaches the A site → release factors enter → the protein is released.
  • Polysomes: multiple ribosomes simultaneously translate the same mRNA → greater protein production.
  • ✏️ Fill in: The incoming tRNA arrives at the ___ (A) site. The peptide bond forms at the ___ (P) site. The empty tRNA exits through the ___ (E) site. In prokaryotes, initiation depends on the ___ (Shine-Dalgarno) sequence. In eukaryotes, the ___ (5' cap) and the ___ (Kozak) sequence. Stop codons are ___ (UAA, UAG, UGA).
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if a mutation changes the anticodon of a tRNA? That tRNA would deliver its amino acid to the wrong codon → many proteins would have a changed amino acid at specific positions. This can be lethal.
4.6.4.1 Gene regulation in prokaryotes: the lac operon
  • Prokaryotes regulate related genes by grouping them into operons. The E. coli lac operon (Jacob and Monod, 1961) is the classic model.
  • Components: Regulatory gene lacI (encodes the repressor); Promoter (Plac, where RNA polymerase binds); Operator (O, repressor binding site); Structural genes: lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase).
  • Negative regulation — the repressor: without lactose, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription. With lactose (allolactose acts as inducer), the repressor detaches from the operator → genes are transcribed.
  • Positive regulation — CAP/CRP: with low glucose (high cAMP), the CAP (CRP) protein binds the promoter and increases RNA polymerase affinity → more transcription. With high glucose, CAP does not act even if lactose is present.
  • 4 key scenarios (exam questions):
  • ①No glucose + lactose present → genes active (maximum transcription: repressor off + CAP on).
  • ②Glucose present + lactose present → genes transcribe but at a low level (repressor off but CAP inactive).
  • ③No glucose + no lactose → genes blocked (repressor on).
  • ④Glucose present + no lactose → genes blocked (repressor on + CAP inactive).
  • ✏️ Fill in: The gene encoding the lac operon repressor is ___ (lacI). The repressor binds the ___ (operator). The molecule that acts as inducer is ___ (allolactose). The positive regulatory protein is ___ (CAP/CRP). When glucose is low, the level of ___ (cAMP) increases.
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if the lac operon operator has a mutation that prevents the repressor from binding? The lacZ, lacY and lacA genes would be transcribed constitutively (always on), even without lactose present. This wastes cellular resources.
4.6.4.2 Gene regulation in eukaryotes
  • Gene regulation in eukaryotes can occur at multiple levels:
  • ①Chromatin: chromatin packaging (heterochromatin vs euchromatin) and histone modifications (acetylation activates; methylation can silence).
  • ②Transcription: transcription factors can activate or inhibit specific genes; enhancers can be far from the promoter.
  • ③RNA processing: alternative splicing allows different proteins to be obtained from the same gene.
  • ④Translation: miRNA (microRNA) blocks translation or induces mRNA degradation.
  • ⑤Post-translational: ubiquitination marks proteins for degradation by the proteasome; phosphorylation activates/inactivates proteins.
  • Key: different cells have the same DNA but express different genes. Differential regulation explains cell specialization (how a neuron and a muscle cell are so different despite having the same genome).
  • 🔬 Scenario: Why can two cells with the same DNA be so different? Because they differentially regulate which genes are expressed. Transcription factors, chromatin structure and miRNAs determine the expression profile of each cell type.
4.7 DNA technology
  • PCR amplifies specific sequences from minimal amounts.
  • Recombinant DNA: cut (endonucleases) + insert into vector → host cell.
  • GMOs, gene therapy, sequencing, genomics → medical and agricultural applications.
  • Bioethics: risks, access and responsible use.
4.8 Biotechnology
  • Definition: biotechnology is the use of organisms, cells or biological molecules to produce food, medicines and other goods.
  • Traditional biotechnology: use of yeasts to make bread, beer and wine; selective breeding of plants; selective breeding of animals.
  • Modern biotechnology: uses genetic engineering; refers to more direct methods for altering DNA; genes can be deleted, added or changed.
  • Key definition: recombinant DNA = DNA containing genes or parts of genes from two or more organisms. Modern biotechnology uses recombinant DNA.
  • Restriction enzymes and ligases: restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences; ligases join DNA fragments. Some restriction enzymes generate "sticky ends" (single-stranded cohesive ends) that facilitate joining with other fragments.
  • Recombinant DNA in nature: sexual reproduction recombines DNA; in meiosis I homologous chromosomes exchange DNA (crossing over); bacteria can take up DNA from the environment by transformation; some viruses can transfer DNA between species.
  • Key definition: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) is a technique that amplifies a DNA segment. It can produce billions of copies of selected DNA fragments. Applications: forensics, cloning, production of transgenic organisms, diagnosis, analysis of DNA from crime scenes.
  • Gel electrophoresis: technique to separate DNA segments by size by applying an electric field to the gel.
  • STR (Short Tandem Repeats): short repeated sequences scattered throughout the genome; used to identify individuals with high precision in forensic laboratories.
  • DNA probes: used in hybridization techniques to label specific nucleotide sequences (detect the presence of a gene or target sequence).
  • CRISPR-Cas9: modern tool that allows precise DNA editing (cutting and modifying genes at a specific site).
  • Key definition: a GMO (genetically modified organism) is a plant, animal or microorganism whose DNA has been modified through genetic engineering.
  • Steps to produce a GMO: 1) obtain the desired gene, 2) clone the gene, 3) insert the gene into the host organism's cells.
  • Obtaining the desired gene: DNA can be isolated from cells; cut with restriction enzymes; separated by gel electrophoresis; or synthesized chemically.
  • Molecular cloning: involves inserting a gene into a bacterial plasmid; that plasmid replicates when the bacterium multiplies → many copies of the gene are obtained.
  • Inserting the gene into the host: bacteria or viruses as vectors; biolistics ("gene gun"); chemical transfection; injection of foreign DNA into fertilized eggs.
  • Examples of transgenic organisms: modified corn, cotton and soy; crops resistant to insects or herbicides; Bt cotton plants (insecticidal toxin); animals modified to produce more wool, more milk protein or less fat.
  • Genomics: study of the complete genome of an organism (structure, function and evolution of genes).
  • Human Genome Project: the human genome contains approximately 20,000 genes; those genes comprise approximately 2% of the DNA; much of the rest is non-coding DNA.
  • Medical impact: understanding the genome has a great impact on medicine; many human diseases are caused by defective alleles; PCR is a diagnostic tool; DNA probes are also used.
  • Key definition: gene therapy is the attempt to cure diseases by inserting, deleting or altering genes in a patient's cells.
  • Common mistake: PCR amplifies DNA, it does not modify it.
  • Common mistake: molecular cloning (copying a gene into a plasmid) is NOT the same as cloning a whole organism.
  • Common mistake: "recombinant DNA" does not mean any spontaneous mutation; it involves combining DNA from two or more organisms in the laboratory (or through specific biological processes such as transformation or viruses).
  • Applications by field: medicine (PCR/probe diagnosis, gene therapy, production of human insulin in bacteria), forensics (STR analysis, crime scenes, paternity testing), agriculture (pest/herbicide-resistant crops, higher yield, better nutritional value).

Topic 5. Evolution of life
Evolutionary thought, population genetics, Hardy-Weinberg, selection, speciation.
T5
5.1 Principles of evolution
  • Definition: evolution is the change that occurs over time in the characteristics of populations.
  • Earlier traditional view: early biological studies did not include the concept of evolution; it was thought that all organisms were created simultaneously and that species remained unchanged.
  • Observations of naturalists: the diversity of life was greater than thought; each region had its own set of species; some local species resembled each other closely; fossils of organisms now extinct were discovered. These observations conflicted with the idea of immutable species.
  • Lamarck: proposed an evolutionary mechanism based on the inheritance of acquired characteristics: the use and disuse of structures modifies them during an individual's lifetime, and those modifications are passed on to offspring. Important: Lamarck proposed an evolutionary mechanism, but did NOT propose natural selection.
  • Darwin: traveled on the Beagle; observed species in many habitats; arrived at the Galápagos in 1835.
  • Galápagos finches: Darwin observed several finch species with different beaks, each associated with a type of food (hard seeds, insects, nectar, etc.). Beak size and shape are related to efficient exploitation of the available food resource.
  • Darwin and Wallace: the theory of evolution by natural selection was presented by Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace in 1858.
  • Four postulates of Darwin and Wallace:
    1. Individuals vary within a population.
    2. Characteristics are inherited from parents to offspring.
    3. Some individuals do not survive or reproduce.
    4. Survival and reproduction are not determined by chance.
  • Postulate 1 — Individual variation: each individual has a unique combination of traits; differences exist in size, color, environmental tolerance, resistance to parasites or infections; variation extends down to the level of DNA.
  • Postulate 2 — Inheritance: variation is heritable; Mendel showed that traits can be transmitted to offspring through hereditary factors (genes).
  • Postulate 3 — Overproduction: each species can produce more offspring than survive; populations tend to remain relatively stable; overproduction exists: more organisms must be born than survive to reproduce.
  • Postulate 4 — Non-random reproductive success: reproductive success depends on an individual's traits; those with favorable combinations survive more and leave more offspring. Class examples: larger elephant seals dominate harems and leave more offspring; snapdragon plants with flowers that attract pollinators better; antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive treatment and proliferate.
  • Natural selection: the process by which nature "selects" individuals with advantageous traits; they survive more and leave more offspring, thus modifying populations over time.
  • Key idea: an individual does NOT evolve; a population DOES. The individual is born with its genotype and dies with it; what changes over time are the frequencies of traits within the population.
  • Evidence of evolution: evidence comes from fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biochemistry and genetics.
  • Fossils: show progressive series; new species appear from prior species. Example: evolution of whales from terrestrial ancestors with limbs, through semi-aquatic forms, to today's fully aquatic whales.
  • Comparative anatomy: comparison of the bodies of different organisms; similarities are explained by common ancestry; body structures modified for different functions.
  • Homologous structures: structures with the same evolutionary origin, even though they may have different functions (e.g. human arm, bat wing, whale flipper → same bone plan).
  • Vestigial structures: inherited structures that appear to have no defined purpose or have reduced function. Examples: remnants of hind limbs in whales and boas (reduced hip and femur bones with no locomotor function).
  • Convergent evolution: natural selection can cause non-homologous structures with similar functions to come to resemble each other closely.
  • Analogous structures: structures that are externally or functionally similar, but with different evolutionary origin (e.g. insect wing and bird wing: same function, different origin).
  • Embryology: vertebrate embryos show a remarkable resemblance in their early stages (pharyngeal arches, tail, segmentation), providing evidence of common ancestry.
  • Biochemical and genetic evidence: molecular similarity among species; existence of homologous molecules; similarities in DNA sequences (the closer the relationship, the greater the similarity).
  • Universal biochemical similarities: all cells use DNA, RNA, ribosomes, nearly the same genetic code, approximately the same 20 amino acids, and ATP as energy carrier → strong evidence of common origin.
  • Artificial selection: observable evidence that populations can change through selective breeding in domestic plants and animals (dog breeds, corn varieties, dairy cattle) → demonstrates that selection generates change in just a few generations.
  • Common mistake: Lamarck did NOT propose natural selection (that was Darwin and Wallace).
  • Common mistake: homologous and analogous are NOT the same. Homologous = same origin; analogous = same function but different origin.
  • Common mistake: evolution does NOT happen because an organism "wants to change" or "needs to". Variations exist at random; selection acts on what already exists.
  • Common mistake: do NOT confuse evolution of the individual with evolution of the population. Only populations evolve.
5.1.1 History of evolutionary thought and Darwin
  • In ancient views the idea of fixed and immutable species predominated.
  • Lamarck proposed an evolutionary mechanism based on use and disuse and inheritance of acquired traits.
  • Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection as the main mechanism of evolutionary change.
  • Darwin gathered observations on biogeography, fossils and variation in organisms, including the Galápagos finches.
  • Mistake: Lamarck did not propose natural selection.
5.1.2 Synthetic theory of evolution
  • The synthetic theory integrates Mendelian genetics, mutation, recombination, natural selection and population evolution.
  • Evolution is understood as change in allele frequencies over time.
  • It unites hereditary mechanisms with the evolutionary change observed in populations.
  • Key: the synthetic theory connects genetics and evolution.
5.1.3 Evidence of evolution
  • Evolution is supported by fossils, comparative anatomy, embryology, biogeography, biochemistry and genetics.
  • Homologous structures indicate common ancestry; analogous structures reflect convergent evolution.
  • Vestigial structures support the idea of evolutionary change.
  • Molecular similarities between species reflect evolutionary relatedness.
  • Mistake: homologous and analogous are not equivalent.
5.2.1 Population genetics
  • Studies the distribution of alleles and genotypes in a population.
  • Evolution, at this level, consists of changes in allele frequencies over time.
  • The set of alleles of a population constitutes its gene pool.
  • Mutation, selection, genetic drift and gene flow can modify that pool.
  • Key: population evolution = change in allele frequencies, not individual change.
  • Calculation: may require interpreting allele and genotype frequencies.
5.2.2 Hardy-Weinberg
  • p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Heterozygotes = 2pq.
  • 5 conditions: no mutation, no selection, random mating, no migration, large population size.
  • Key: if the population deviates from equilibrium → evolution is acting.
  • Describes the expected genetic equilibrium in an ideal population.
  • If p is the frequency of one allele and q that of the other, then p + q = 1.
  • The expected genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q².
  • If a population deviates from equilibrium, some evolutionary force is acting.
  • Step-by-step worked example: Suppose the frequency of allele a in a population is q = 0.3.
    Step 1 — Find p: p = 1 − q = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.
    Step 2 — Calculate genotype frequencies:
       • Dominant homozygotes AA = p² = 0.7² = 0.49 (49%).
       • Heterozygotes Aa = 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42 (42%).
       • Recessive homozygotes aa = q² = 0.3² = 0.09 (9%).
    Step 3 — Verification: 0.49 + 0.42 + 0.09 = 1.00 ✓.
    Step 4 — Interpretation: if in the real population 12% are aa instead of the expected 9%, the frequency of q is increasing → some evolutionary force is acting. Common mistake: forgetting that aa = q² (not q). To find q from the frequency of recessive aa, take the square root: q = √(frequency of aa).
  • Calculation: may require finding p, q, p², 2pq, q², frequency of heterozygotes or carriers.
5.2.3 Adaptive changes in allele frequencies
  • If an allele improves survival or reproduction, it can increase its frequency in the population.
  • Natural selection favors advantageous heritable combinations in a specific environment.
  • When the environment changes, which traits are favorable can also change.
  • Adaptations arise through selection on existing variation, not through the organism's conscious need.
  • Mistake: adaptive does not mean "desired" or "sought" by the organism.
5.2.4–5 Evolutionary forces and types of selection
  • Mutation is the original source of new alleles; without it there is no heritable variation.
  • Genetic drift produces random changes in allele frequencies, especially strong in small populations. Cases: founder effect (few individuals form a new population) and bottleneck (drastic reduction of the population).
  • Gene flow occurs when individuals or gametes move between populations → homogenizes allele frequencies and introduces new alleles.
  • Inbreeding and non-random mating change genotype frequencies (more homozygotes) but not necessarily allele frequencies.
  • Key: not all evolutionary changes are due to natural selection. Drift, gene flow and mutation also alter the gene pool.
ForceMechanismEffect on the gene pool
MutationChanges in the DNA sequenceCreates new alleles (original source)
Natural selectionDifferential survival/reproductionIncreases advantageous alleles (non-random)
Genetic driftRandom sampling of gametesChanges frequencies at random; strong if N is small
Gene flowMigration of individuals or gametesHomogenizes populations; introduces new alleles
Non-random matingMate choice, inbreedingChanges genotype frequencies, not allele frequencies; increases homozygosity
Type of selectionWhat it favorsExample
StabilizingThe average phenotype; eliminates extremes; the distribution narrowsHuman birth weight (very low or very high → lower survival)
DirectionalOne extreme of the range; shifts the mean of the distributionPeppered moth during the Industrial Revolution; finch beaks after drought
DisruptiveBoth extremes; the average phenotype is at a disadvantage; bimodal distributionFinches with very large or very small beaks when only seeds of extreme sizes exist
5.2.6 Sexual selection
  • Favors traits that increase mating success, even if they do not always improve survival.
  • It can act through competition among individuals of the same sex or through mate choice.
  • Explains ornaments, courtship behaviors and sexual dimorphism in many species.
  • Key: evolutionary success also depends on leaving offspring.
5.2.7 Artificial selection
  • Occurs when humans choose which individuals reproduce based on desired traits.
  • It has given rise to domestic breeds and agricultural varieties with very marked characteristics.
  • Shows that a population can change in a few generations if reproduction is not random.
  • Mistake: artificial selection is not the same as natural selection; the selective agent changes.
5.3.1 The biological species concept
  • According to the biological concept, a species is a set of populations whose individuals can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
  • Reproductive isolation contributes to keeping species separate.
  • This concept works best in organisms with sexual reproduction.
  • Mistake: physical resemblance is not enough to belong to the same species.
5.3 Speciation
  • Prezygotic reproductive isolation (prevents fertilization): Ecological (different habitats), Temporal (different breeding seasons), Behavioral (different courtship), Mechanical (anatomical incompatibility), Gametic (gametes do not recognize each other).
  • Postzygotic reproductive isolation (fertilization occurs but offspring fail): Inviability of the zygote or embryo; Hybrid sterility (classic example: the mule, a cross between a horse and a donkey, is viable but sterile); Loss of fertility in subsequent generations.
  • Types of speciation by geography:
  • → Allopatric: geographic separation by a physical barrier (river, mountain, glacier). The most common. Each subpopulation accumulates different mutations and experiences different selective pressures.
  • → Sympatric: in the same geographic space, without a barrier. Mechanisms: ecological divergence, assortative mating and especially polyploidy in plants.
  • → Parapatric: contiguous areas with limited gene flow in the contact zone. Divergent selection in each habitat.
  • → Peripatric: a special case of allopatric where a small population becomes isolated at the periphery → strong genetic drift (founder effect).
  • Polyploidy as instantaneous sympatric speciation: Autopolyploidy = duplication of the chromosome set of a single species. Allopolyploidy = hybridization between two species + chromosome duplication. Example: modern wheat (Triticum aestivum, hexaploid 6n) arose through hybridization and polyploidization.
  • Key: a polyploid crossed with the original species produces 3n offspring → sterile (meiosis with odd chromosomes impossible) → instant reproductive isolation.
  • Anagenesis = linear transformation of one species into another. Cladogenesis = one species splits into two (branching) → mechanism that increases biodiversity.
  • ✏️ Fill in: Speciation with a geographic barrier is ___ (allopatric). Without a barrier, in the same space, ___ (sympatric). The chromosome duplication that produces instant speciation is ___ (polyploidy). The branching of one species into two is ___ (cladogenesis). A polyploid crossed with the diploid species produces ___ offspring (3n, sterile).
  • 🔬 Scenario: What would happen if a population of lizards is divided by a new river? Each subpopulation accumulates different mutations and faces different selective pressures. After thousands of generations, if they come into contact again they may no longer interbreed → complete allopatric speciation.
  • 🔬 Scenario: Why does polyploidy produce nearly instantaneous reproductive isolation? Because crossing a polyploid (4n) with the original species (2n) produces 3n offspring, which cannot undergo meiosis correctly (odd chromosomes without a partner) → sterile hybrids. Polyploids only reproduce among themselves.
5.3.4 Macroevolution, extinction and evolutionary rate
  • Macroevolution analyzes evolutionary patterns at the species level or above (genera, families, classes).
  • It includes the origin of major groups, adaptive radiations (rapid diversification when reaching a new environment or after extinction) and long-term changes in biodiversity.
  • Extinction eliminates lineages and modifies evolutionary history. Mass extinctions can open niches for new radiations. Example: extinction of non-avian dinosaurs 66 Ma ago opened the way for the radiation of mammals.
  • Gradualism (Darwin): slow and continuous change over time.
  • Punctuated equilibrium (Eldredge and Gould): long periods of stability (stasis) interrupted by rapid evolutionary changes associated with speciation.
  • Key: accumulated microevolutionary processes (changes in allele frequencies) contribute to macroevolutionary patterns (origin of new species and clades).
6
Topic 6. Biological diversity
Origin of life and first cells (6.1). Topics 6.2–6.4 correspond to Unit 3.
T6
6.1 Origin of life
  • Miller-Urey: abiotic synthesis of amino acids under primitive conditions (no O₂).
  • Chemical evolution: simple compounds → macromolecules → protocells.
  • First cells: anaerobic heterotrophic prokaryotes.
  • Cyanobacteria → O₂ into the atmosphere. Endosymbiosis → mitochondria and chloroplasts.
6.1.1 Main stages: formation of the planet
  • The primitive Earth formed billions of years ago under conditions very different from today's.
  • It had strong volcanic activity, high temperatures, intense radiation and frequent electrical storms.
  • The primitive atmosphere had a different composition and almost no free oxygen.
  • These conditions inform the hypotheses about chemical evolution and the origin of life.
  • Key: the origin of life is studied within the physicochemical context of the primitive planet.
6.1.2 Theories of the origin of life
  • Modern abiogenesis proposes that life arose from non-living matter through gradual physicochemical processes.
  • Oparin and Haldane suggested that simple molecules could give rise to more complex organic compounds.
  • Other proposals explore environments such as hydrothermal vents and prebiotic synthesis in different scenarios.
  • The aim of these theories is to explain the origin of biological systems from natural processes.
  • Mistake: a theory of the origin of life does not mean the complete formation of a cell has already been observed in the laboratory.
6.1.3 Formation of macromolecules, protocells and first cells
  • Simple organic molecules could give rise to macromolecules with increasingly complex functions.
  • Protocells would have been aggregates with rudimentary membranes and some internal chemical organization.
  • The first cells were probably anaerobic heterotrophic prokaryotes.
  • Later, photosynthetic organisms appeared that contributed to the increase of atmospheric oxygen.
  • Key: a protocell is not equivalent to a complete modern cell; it represents a prior stage.

BottleneckDrastic reduction in population size; intensifies genetic drift
DeletionLoss of a DNA or chromosomal fragment
Genetic driftRandom change in allele frequencies; especially strong if N is small
Diploid (2n)Two copies of each chromosome (somatic cells; humans: 2n=46)

📚 Theory summary — Third unit

Organisation of information about species, biological diversity (viruses, prions, prokaryotes, protists, plants, fungi, invertebrate animals and chordates) and ecology (populations, communities, ecosystems and biosphere). Identical structure to P1/P2: collapsible sections by subtopic, with key ideas and common mistakes highlighted.

6
Topic 6 — Organisation of information about species and biological diversity
Systematics, taxonomy, viruses/prions, prokaryotes, protists, plants, fungi, invertebrate animals and chordates
Summary
6.2 Systematics, taxonomy and the tree of life (6.2.1 – 6.2.4)
  • 6.2.1 Systematic biology: integrates classification + phylogeny + diversity. It is not just "naming things" — that is taxonomy.
  • Taxon: any recognised group in the hierarchy (species, genus, family, domain).
  • Clade: common ancestor + ALL its descendants (monophyletic group). If a descendant is excluded, it is not a valid clade.
  • 6.2.2.1 Linnaeus hierarchy (8 levels): Domain → Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. Higher = broader and more diverse; lower = more specific.
  • 6.2.2.2 Binomial system: Genus (capitalised) + specific epithet (lowercase), in italics. E.g.: Homo sapiens, Escherichia coli.
  • 6.2.3 Tools: comparative anatomy, embryology, fossil record, molecular evidence (DNA/RNA). Ribosomal RNA → basis of the three-domain system.
  • Homology vs Analogy: homology = same origin, different function (e.g. bat wing and human arm); analogy = same function, different origin (e.g. insect wing and bird wing).
  • 6.2.3.1 Phylogenetic trees: node = hypothetical ancestor; branch = diverging lineage; root = oldest ancestor. Visual position (up/down) does NOT indicate "more evolved".
  • 6.2.4 Carl Woese (1977): 16S ribosomal RNA → discovered that prokaryotes are not a homogeneous group → three domains: Bacteria + Archaea + Eukarya.
Concept What it does Question it answers
TaxonomyNames and classifies"What is it called and where does it belong?"
PhylogeneticsReconstructs evolutionary relationships"Where does it come from and who is it related to?"
SystematicsIntegrates both within the study of diversity"How is all this diversity organised evolutionarily?"
Trait Bacteria Archaea Eukarya
True nucleusNoNoYes
Cell wallWith peptidoglycanNo peptidoglycan (pseudopeptidoglycan)Variable or absent
Membrane lipidsEsterEther (unique in life)Ester
Bacterial antibioticsYes (sensitive)No (resistant)No
Histones on DNANoYes (similar to eukaryotes)Yes
⚠️ Exam traps: (1) Systematics ≠ taxonomy ≠ phylogenetics — not interchangeable. (2) "Reptilia" without birds is NOT a clade (paraphyletic). (3) Position on a phylogenetic tree does not mean "more evolved". (4) Archaea is NOT a type of bacterium. (5) "homo Sapiens" is incorrect — must be Homo sapiens.
🔬 Scenario: Unicellular organism with no nucleus, no peptidoglycan, ether lipids, lives at 90°C. Bacterium or Archaea? A: Archaea. No-peptidoglycan + ether lipids are diagnostic for Archaea, not Bacteria.
🔬 Phylogenetic tree scenario: A and B share a node; that node connects to C at an older node. Who is most closely related? A: A and B with each other — they share a more recent common ancestor than either shares with C.
6.3.1 Structure and characteristics of viruses — Lytic and lysogenic cycles
  • Viruses are acellular entities: genetic material (DNA or RNA, never both) + protein capsid. Some have a host-membrane envelope.
  • They are not cells: no cytoplasm, ribosomes, or metabolism of their own → obligate intracellular parasites. They infect all domains; those of bacteria = bacteriophages.
  • Lytic cycle: replicates immediately → lysis → cell dies → releases hundreds of new viruses.
  • Lysogenic cycle: viral genome integrates into the host chromosome as a prophage → cell survives and divides normally for many generations → stress (UV) can induce the prophage to enter the lytic cycle.
Feature Lytic cycle Lysogenic cycle
Replicates immediately?YesNo (remains integrated)
State of viral genomeActive, replicatingIntegrated as prophage
Does the cell die?Yes, by lysisNot immediately; can survive for generations
Produces viral particles?Yes, hundredsNo, until activated
Lysogenic → lytic trigger—Cell stress (UV radiation, chemicals)
🔬 Step-by-step process: Lytic cycle (5 stages)

1. Adsorption: the virus recognises specific receptors on the host surface and binds. 2. Penetration: the viral genetic material enters the cell (in phages, the capsid remains outside). 3. Biosynthesis: the viral genome hijacks the cell's machinery to replicate and produce viral proteins. 4. Assembly (maturation): the genome is packaged into newly synthesised capsids. 5. Release by lysis: viral enzymes break the cell wall, the cell bursts and releases viral particles into the environment.

⚠️ Exam traps: (1) Not every virus destroys the cell immediately — in the lysogenic cycle it can remain inactive for generations. (2) Virus ≠ small cell. (3) Viruses do not belong to any classical biological kingdom (they are acellular).
🔬 Scenario: A bacterium with an integrated prophage is exposed to UV radiation. What do you predict? A: The prophage activates → lysogenic→lytic transition → actively replicates → lyses the bacterium.
6.3.2 Viroids and prions — Non-cellular infectious agents
Agent Composition Coat Typical host
VirusNucleic acid (DNA or RNA) + proteinYes (capsid)All domains
ViroidShort, circular, naked RNANoPlants (crops)
PrionMisfolded protein (no nucleic acid)NoAnimals (neurodegenerative diseases)

Prions are revolutionary: they transmit "information" through protein conformation, without nucleic acid. E.g.: "mad cow disease" (bovine spongiform encephalopathy), Creutzfeldt-Jakob.

⚠️ Exam trap: Viroids and prions are NOT types of viruses. They are agents with completely different chemical natures.
🔬 Scenario: An infectious agent resistant to nucleases (which destroy nucleic acids) but sensitive to proteases. What type is it? A: Prion — its nature is exclusively proteinaceous.
6.3.3–6.3.6 Prokaryotes: structure, bacteria, archaea and reproduction
  • Prokaryotes: no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles. Circular DNA in a nucleoid, 70S ribosomes. "Prokaryote" ≠ "bacterium" (Archaea are also prokaryotes).
  • Bacteria: cell wall with peptidoglycan. Classified by shape (cocci, bacilli, spirilla), staining (Gram +/−), metabolism.
  • Gram-positive staining (purple): thick peptidoglycan wall retains crystal violet. Gram-negative (pink): thin wall + outer membrane with lipopolysaccharides (LPS = endotoxins) → alcohol washes out crystal violet.
  • Special structures: flagella (locomotion), biofilms (adherent communities), endospores (extreme resistance — not reproduction).
  • Archaea: no peptidoglycan (pseudopeptidoglycan), ether-linked lipids, complex RNA polymerase. Not all are extremophiles. Closer to Eukarya than to Bacteria in molecular phylogeny.
  • Reproduction: binary fission (asexual). E. coli divides every 20 min under optimal conditions.
HGT mechanism How it works Vehicle
TransformationBacterium takes up free DNA from the environment (from a dead bacterium)Free DNA
TransductionBacteriophage accidentally transports bacterial DNA from one cell to anotherVirus (phage)
ConjugationDonor cell transfers plasmid to recipient via sex pilus (direct contact)Pilus / plasmid
🔬 Step-by-step process: Bacterial conjugation

1. Donor bacterium extends sex pilus toward recipient. 2. Pilus retracts → direct contact → cytoplasmic bridge. 3. Donor plasmid is nicked and one strand is transferred by rolling-circle replication. 4. In the recipient, the complementary strand is synthesised and the plasmid recircularises. 5. Both cells end up carrying the plasmid. If it contains resistance genes → both are resistant. Conjugation allows resistance to spread between different species, explaining the speed of propagation.

⚠️ Exam traps: (1) Conjugation is NOT "bacterial sex" (no gametic fusion or meiosis). (2) Bacterial conjugation ≠ conjugation in Paramecium. (3) Archaea is NOT a subclass of Bacteria. (4) Not all archaea are extremophiles. (5) Endospore = resistance structure, NOT reproduction.
🔬 Scenario: A Gram-positive bacterium loses the ability to synthesise peptidoglycan by mutation. What happens? A: Loses osmotic support → lyses easily. Stops retaining crystal violet (no longer Gram+). Becomes unaffected by penicillin (which acts by inhibiting peptidoglycan synthesis). Analogous mechanism to penicillin's action.
🔬 Conjugation scenario: An ampicillin-sensitive bacterium is mixed with a resistant one carrying the resistance gene on a plasmid. After some time, the formerly sensitive bacteria are also resistant. What happened? A: Conjugation: the plasmid carrying the resistance gene was transferred by direct contact.
6.4.1–6.4.2 Biology of protists and serial endosymbiosis
  • Protists are highly heterogeneous eukaryotes — they do not group with plants, animals, or fungi.
  • Mostly unicellular; some colonial or simply multicellular. Predominantly aquatic or moist habitats.
  • Varied nutrition: autotrophs, heterotrophs, or mixotrophs (switch strategy depending on the environment).
  • Critical concept: "Protist" is NOT a valid clade — it is a paraphyletic convenience group. Animals, plants, and fungi are phylogenetically "nested" among the protists.
OrganelleAncestral bacterium (endosymbiosis)
MitochondrionAlpha-proteobacteria (aerobic)
ChloroplastCyanobacteria (oxygenic photosynthetic)

6 lines of evidence for endosymbiosis (frequently examined):

  • Double membrane — the outer one comes from the phagocytosis event; the inner one is the original bacterial membrane.
  • Own circular DNA — similar to bacterial DNA, lacking histones like nuclear DNA.
  • 70S ribosomes — bacterial type, not 80S like the rest of the eukaryotic cell.
  • Division by binary fission — independent of the host cell division.
  • Size — comparable to that of present-day bacteria.
  • DNA sequences — mitochondrial and chloroplast DNA phylogenetically cluster with specific bacteria.
🔬 Process — Origin of mitochondria and chloroplasts by endosymbiosis
  1. Large ancestral cell (proto-eukaryote / archaeal) capable of phagocytosing other cells.
  2. Phagocytoses an aerobic alpha-proteobacterium → instead of digesting it, keeps it alive inside.
  3. A mutually beneficial relationship is established: the bacterium provides ATP (aerobic respiration), the cell provides protection and nutrients.
  4. Over millions of years, the bacterium loses unnecessary genes, transfers its genetic material to the nucleus → becomes a mitochondrion.
  5. Later event: a eukaryotic cell already with mitochondria phagocytoses a photosynthetic cyanobacterium → same process → chloroplast.
⚠️ Exam traps:
• "Protist is an evolutionarily valid kingdom" → FALSE, it is a paraphyletic group.
• "All protists are microscopic" → FALSE. Brown algae (kelps) can reach 30+ m.
• "All organelles arose through endosymbiosis" → FALSE. Nucleus, ER, and Golgi arose by membrane invagination. Only mitochondria and chloroplasts have a clear endosymbiotic origin.
🧠 Scenario: A new organelle is discovered in a protist with a double membrane, circular DNA, and 70S ribosomes. What hypothesis arises? A: Endosymbiotic origin from a bacterium.
6.4.3–6.4.5 Ecological role, diversity and protist groups
Ecological roleExamples
Aquatic producers (phytoplankton)Diatoms, dinoflagellates, green algae
Aquatic consumers (zooplankton)Ciliates, foraminifera
ParasitesPlasmodium (malaria), Trypanosoma (Chagas), Giardia
SymbiontsZooxanthellae in corals (build reefs)

Phytoplankton produces ≈ 50% of the world's atmospheric oxygen and forms the base of marine food webs.

MotilityMechanismExample
CiliaShort, coordinated beatsParamecium
FlagellaLong whip-like strokesEuglena, Trypanosoma
PseudopodsCytoplasmic extensionsAmoebas
No evident locomotionSedentary forms or intracellular parasitesSome obligate parasites
Traditional groupFeaturesExamples
Animal-like (protozoa)Heterotrophic, motileAmoebas, ciliates, flagellates
Plant-like (algae)PhotosyntheticDiatoms, green, red, and brown algae
Fungus-likeHeterotrophic, absorptive, sporesSlime moulds, water moulds
⚠️ Trap: These groupings are practical, NOT phylogenetic. Modern systematics uses supergroups (Excavata, SAR, Archaeplastida, Amoebozoa). The course uses traditional classification for simplicity.
6.5.1–6.5.2 Origin, adaptations and alternation of generations
  • Land plants evolved from ancestral green algae (charophytes) — they share chloroplasts with chlorophyll a and b, starch, and cellulose cell walls.
  • Central evolutionary challenge: colonisation of land imposed problems that water solved "for free".
Problem on landEvolutionary solution
DesiccationCuticle (impermeable waxy layer)
Gas exchange without water lossStomata with guard cells
Body support (no buoyancy)Lignin, vascular tissues
Internal transport of water and nutrientsXylem (water and minerals ↑) + Phloem (sugars in both directions)
Anchorage and soil absorptionRoots
Reproduction without free waterPollen, seeds
Dispersal of offspringFruits (angiosperms only)

Alternation of generations (fundamental concept):

PhasePloidyProduces
GametophyteHaploid (n)Gametes by mitosis
SporophyteDiploid (2n)Spores by meiosis
GroupDominant phaseWater dependence
BryophytesDominant gametophyteHigh — sperm must swim
Ferns (seedless vascular)Dominant sporophyteMedium — small but free-living gametophyte
Gymnosperms + AngiospermsHighly dominant sporophyte; gametophyte reduced to a few cellsLow — pollen carries gametes without water
🔬 Process — Alternation of generations (full narrative)
  1. Begins with a haploid spore (n) that germinates and divides by mitosis → multicellular haploid gametophyte.
  2. The gametophyte produces gametes by mitosis (already haploid): sperm and eggs.
  3. Fertilisation: fusion of gametes → diploid zygote (2n).
  4. The zygote divides by mitosis → multicellular diploid sporophyte.
  5. The sporophyte produces spores by meiosis in sporangia → haploid spores → cycle restarts.

Evolutionary trend: progressive reduction of the gametophyte and increasing dominance of the sporophyte → less dependence on water for reproduction.

⚠️ Exam traps:
• "Bryophytes are still very tied to water for reproduction" → TRUE (reverse trap: confusing with gymnosperms).
• "All plants have the same level of terrestrial adaptation" → FALSE.
• "The gametophyte produces spores" → FALSE. The sporophyte produces spores (by meiosis); the gametophyte produces gametes (by mitosis).
🧠 Scenario: A plant has a large, green gametophyte and a small sporophyte that grows on it and depends on it nutritionally. What group is it? A: Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts).
6.5.3 Main taxonomic groups of plants
GroupVascular?Seed?Flower and fruit?Dominant phaseExamples
BryophytesNoNoNoGametophyteMosses, liverworts, hornworts
Seedless vascularYesNoNoSporophyteFerns, club mosses, horsetails
GymnospermsYesYes (naked)NoSporophytePines, cypresses, firs, sequoias
AngiospermsYesYes (in fruit)YesSporophyteOak, maize, apple, orchid

Each level = accumulated evolutionary innovation: 1) Vascular tissue → greater size. 2) Seed → reproduction without water + nutritive reserve. 3) Flower and fruit → directed pollination + animal dispersal.

Innovations exclusive to angiosperms:

  • Double fertilisation: one sperm → egg cell → embryo (2n); the other → two polar nuclei → endosperm (3n).
  • Endosperm: triploid (3n) nutritive tissue that feeds the embryo. Gymnosperms lack true endosperm.
  • Vessel elements in xylem (more efficient than the tracheids of gymnosperms).
🔬 Process — Double fertilisation in angiosperms
  1. Pollen grain reaches the stigma (by wind, insect, bird, or bat).
  2. Pollen germinates → pollen tube grows through the style toward the ovary, carrying two sperm nuclei.
  3. The pollen tube reaches the ovule (embryo sac with egg cell + two polar nuclei).
  4. First fertilisation: sperm nucleus + egg cell (n) → zygote (2n) → embryo.
  5. Second fertilisation: second sperm nucleus + two polar nuclei → triploid nucleus (3n) → endosperm.
  6. Ovule → seed (embryo + endosperm + coat); ovary matures → fruit.
⚠️ Exam traps:
• GYMNOsperms = gymnous/naked seeds (no fruit). ANGIOsperms = seeds IN fruit.
• Confusing endosperm (3n, angiosperms) with the nutritive tissue of gymnosperms (they are different things).
🧠 Scenario: If all angiosperms disappeared, what would happen to pollinators? A: Massive collapse. Most pollinators (bees, butterflies, hummingbirds, bats) depend on flowers. Gymnosperms (mostly wind-pollinated) cannot sustain them.
6.6.1–6.6.2 Characteristics and life cycle of fungi
TraitFungiPlantsAnimals
NutritionHeterotrophic by absorptionAutotrophic (photosynthesis)Heterotrophic by ingestion
Cell wallYes, of chitinYes, of celluloseNone
BodyHyphae → myceliumTrue tissuesTrue tissues
RelationshipOpisthokontaArchaeplastidaOpisthokonta (closer to fungi than to plants)
  • Hypha: individual cellular filament (basic unit). Mycelium: interwoven mass of hyphae (body of the fungus). Fruiting body (mushroom): visible reproductive structure — just the tip of the iceberg.
  • Types: saprotrophs (decompose dead matter), parasites (harm living host), mutualistic symbionts (beneficial exchange).

Fungal sexual cycle — dikaryotic phase unique among eukaryotes:

StageWhat happensPloidy
PlasmogamyFusion of cytoplasms of two compatible hyphaeNo nuclear fusion yet
Dikaryotic phaseTwo distinct haploid nuclei per cell (n + n). Can last yearsn + n (peculiar)
KaryogamyFusion of the two nuclei → diploid cell2n
MeiosisReduces to haploid → sexual sporesn
🔬 Process — Fungal sexual life cycle
  1. Two compatible hyphae ("+" and "−" types) come into contact.
  2. Plasmogamy: cytoplasms fuse; nuclei remain separate.
  3. Dikaryotic phase (n+n): two nuclei per cell; can last years in basidiomycetes.
  4. Fruiting body develops; in asci or basidia karyogamy occurs → transient diploid nucleus (2n).
  5. Meiosis → 4 haploid spores (ascospores or basidiospores).
  6. Spores disperse, germinate, and form new haploid hyphae.
⚠️ Exam traps:
• "Fungi are plants" → FALSE. Chitin wall, heterotrophic by absorption, phylogenetically closer to animals.
• "Fertilisation in fungi is the same as in animals" → FALSE. There is an intermediate dikaryotic phase (n+n) between plasmogamy and karyogamy.
• "All fungi reproduce sexually" → FALSE. Imperfect fungi (Deuteromycetes) only have known asexual reproduction.
6.6.3–6.6.4 Taxonomic groups, symbiosis and ecological importance
GroupDiagnostic traitsSexual structureExamples
ChytridsAquatic, flagellated spores (only fungal group with flagella)VariousBatrachochytrium (kills amphibians)
ZygomycetesForm resistant zygosporesZygosporangiumBread moulds (Rhizopus)
GlomeromycetesForm arbuscular mycorrhizae with most land plantsMostly asexualRoot symbionts
AscomycetesSexual spores in an ascusAscus (ascospores)Yeasts, Penicillium, truffles, morels
BasidiomycetesSpores on a basidiumBasidium (basidiospores)Mushrooms, shelf fungi, rusts, smuts
SymbiosisPartnersFungus providesPartner provides
MycorrhizaeFungus + plant rootGreater water and mineral (phosphorus) uptakePhotosynthetic sugars
LichensFungus + green alga or cyanobacteriumStructure, protection, water retentionPhotosynthetic sugars
  • Together with bacteria, fungi are the main decomposers of lignin and cellulose. Without them, forests would be buried in leaf litter.
  • Glomeromycetes were key to the original colonisation of land by plants (~470 M years ago).
  • Lichens: pioneers in primary succession (grow on bare rock), initiate soil formation, indicators of air quality.
  • Human importance: fermentation (bread, beer, wine) — yeasts; antibiotics — penicillin (Penicillium); food — mushrooms, blue cheeses; diseases — candidiasis, ringworm.
⚠️ Trap: Reducing fungi to "decomposers". They are also essential symbionts, pathogens, and industrial producers. | Confusing ascomycete/basidiomycete: ASCOspores in ASCi / BASIDIOspores on BASIDia.
🧠 Scenario: If mycorrhizae completely die off in a forest region, what do you predict? A: Reduced phosphorus and water uptake → plant stress → slower growth → changes in community composition → cascade effects on herbivores and other trophic levels.
6.7.1–6.7.2 Animal characteristics and body plan
  • Animals: heterotrophic multicellular eukaryotes, no cell wall, nutrition by ingestion, true tissues (except basal groups such as sponges), complex embryonic development.
TraitTypesExamples
Germ layersDiploblastic (ecto + endo) / Triploblastic (+ mesoderm)Diploblastic: Cnidarians | Triploblastic: most animals
SymmetryAsymmetric / Radial / BilateralSponges / Cnidarians, adult echinoderms / Most animals
CoelomAcoelomates / Pseudocoelomates / CoelomatesFlatworms / Nematodes / Annelids, molluscs, arthropods, chordates
SegmentationHomonomous (identical rings) / Heteronomous (tagmata)Annelids / Arthropods
FeatureProtostomesDeuterostomes
Fate of blastopore→ mouth→ anus
Embryonic cleavageSpiral and determinateRadial and indeterminate
Coelom formationSchizocoelousEnterocoelous
ExamplesMolluscs, annelids, arthropodsEchinoderms, chordates (humans)
🔬 Process — Gastrulation and formation of germ layers
  1. Zygote → mitotic cleavages → morula (solid sphere) → blastula (hollow sphere with blastocoel).
  2. Gastrulation: cells invaginate → form archenteron (primitive gut), with an opening called the blastopore.
  3. Germ layers are established: diploblastic (ecto + endo); triploblastic (+ mesoderm).
  4. Each layer gives rise to tissues: Ectoderm → epidermis, nervous system. Endoderm → digestive tube, lungs. Mesoderm → muscles, skeleton, circulatory system.
  5. Fate of blastopore defines the lineage: Protostome = mouth; Deuterostome = anus.
⚠️ Exam traps:
• "Animals are defined by motility" → FALSE. Adult sponges are sessile. Motility may be present only in the larva.
• "Echinoderms are simple animals far removed from humans" → FALSE. They are deuterostomes, closer to chordates than to a worm or snail.
• "Invertebrate is an evolutionary clade" → FALSE. It is a paraphyletic group (everything that does NOT have a vertebral column).
🧠 Scenario: In an embryo, the blastopore becomes the anus. Which lineage is it? A: Deuterostome → echinoderm or chordate.
6.7.3 Diagnostic table of invertebrates
PhylumSymmetryLayersCoelomExclusive / diagnostic traitExamples
PoriferaAsymmetricNo true tissues—Choanocytes + pore systemSponges
CnidariaRadialDiploblastic—Cnidocytes (stinging cells); two forms: polyp and medusaJellyfish, corals, hydras
PlatyhelminthesBilateralTriploblasticAcoelomateFlattened body; incomplete digestion (single opening)Planarians, tapeworms, flukes
NematodaBilateralTriploblasticPseudocoelomateCylindrical body, no segmentation, moulted cuticleAscaris, pinworms
MolluscaBilateralTriploblasticCoelomateFoot + mantle + visceral mass; many with shell; radulaSnails, clams, octopuses
AnnelidaBilateralTriploblasticCoelomateHomonomous segmentation (rings); setaeEarthworms, leeches, polychaetes
ArthropodaBilateralTriploblasticCoelomateChitin exoskeleton + jointed appendages + moulting (ecdysis)Insects, arachnids, crustaceans
EchinodermataBilateral (larva) → Pentaradial (adult)TriploblasticCoelomateWater vascular system + calcareous endoskeleton. DeuterostomesStarfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers
  • Arthropods = most diverse animal group (~75% of all described animal species are insects).
  • Echinoderms are deuterostomes → phylogenetically closer to chordates (humans) than to a worm or snail. Adult appearance is misleading.
⚠️ Traps: Only cnidarians have cnidocytes (if there is a stinging cell = cnidarian). | "Invertebrate" is not a clade: it is everything that does NOT have a vertebral column (paraphyletic). | Classifying by external appearance instead of embryological and deep anatomical traits.
🧠 Scenario: Bilateral aquatic animal, segmented, cylindrical, with setae on each segment. What phylum? A: Annelid (polychaete if marine).
6.8.1–6.8.2 Characteristics of chordates and invertebrate groups

Phylum Chordata. The 5 diagnostic traits may be present only in the embryo or larva, not necessarily in the adult:

Chordate traitFunction / Detail
NotochordFlexible dorsal support rod; in vertebrates replaced by the vertebral column during development
Hollow dorsal nerve cordTubular central nervous system (in other animals the nerve cord is ventral and solid)
Pharyngeal slitsIn aquatic animals: gills. In terrestrial tetrapods: only in embryo, modified into middle ear, neck structures, parathyroids
Post-anal tailMuscular extension beyond the anus (in humans only present in the embryo → reduced to the coccyx)
Endostyle (or thyroid in vertebrates)In invertebrate chordates: produces mucus for filter feeding. In vertebrates: evolved into the thyroid gland
Grupo invertebradoCaracterísticasImportancia
Urochordates (tunicates)Sessile adults, reduced chordate traits. Larvae clearly show notochord, dorsal nerve cord and post-anal tailTadpole-like larva: evidence of evolutionary relationship with vertebrates
Cephalochordates (lancelets)Retain all chordate traits in the adult; fish-like body, no skullModel of the ancestral chordate body plan
⚠️ Traps:
• "Only vertebrates are chordates" → FALSE. Urochordates and cephalochordates are chordates without a vertebral column.
• "Chordate traits are always visible in the adult" → FALSE. In tunicates only the larva clearly shows them.
🧠 Scenario: A swimming larva with a notochord and post-anal muscular tail becomes a sessile adult without those traits. What group is it? A: Urochordate (tunicate / ascidian).
6.8.3–6.8.4 Vertebrate groups and evolutionary milestones
GroupKey traitsReproductionThermoregulationExamples
Agnatha (jawless fish)No jaw, cartilaginous skeletonAquaticEctothermLampreys, hagfish
Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fish)Jaw, cartilaginous skeleton, placoid scalesMostly oviparousEctothermSharks, rays
Osteichthyes (bony fish)Bony skeleton, operculum, swim bladderAquatic, mostly oviparousEctothermSalmon, tuna
AmphibiaNaked moist skin, metamorphosisNeed water; unprotected eggsEctothermFrogs, salamanders
ReptiliaKeratinised scales, dry skin, amniotic eggIndependent of waterEctothermTurtles, lizards, snakes
AvesFeathers, hollow bones, amniotic egg with hard shellOviparous; parental careEndothermEagles, penguins
MammaliaHair, mammary glands, 3 middle ear ossicles, diaphragmMostly viviparous; monotremes oviparousEndothermHumans, whales, platypus
Innovation (milestone)Problem solvedWho has it
JawsActive capture and processing of preyGnathostomes (all vertebrates except Agnatha)
Limbs with digitsSupport and terrestrial locomotionTetrapods (amphibians + amniotes)
Amniotic eggReproduction without free water; greater embryonic protectionReptiles, birds, mammals (amniotes)
EndothermySustained activity independent of environmental temperatureBirds and mammals (convergence — evolved twice)
  • "Fish" is not a valid clade: tetrapods descend from bony fish. In strict cladistics, humans are derived "sarcopterygian fish".
  • "Reptiles" is also not a clade: birds descend from theropod dinosaurs. The correct clade is Sauropsida (which includes birds).
  • Endothermy evolved independently in birds and in mammals (evolutionary convergence).
⚠️ Exam traps:
• "A fish turns into an amphibian that turns into a reptile" → FALSE. Evolution is branching, not a linear ladder.
• "Humans are the pinnacle of evolution" → FALSE. All current groups are equally modern in time.
🧠 Scenario: If the amniotic egg had never evolved, which groups would not exist? A: Reptiles, birds, and mammals. Vertebrates would have remained limited to the vicinity of water for reproduction.
