Topic 7 — Ecology
Populations, communities, energy and nutrient flow, major ecosystems of the biosphere
Summary
7.1.1–7.1.2 Ecology and population characteristics

Ecology: the branch that studies interactions among living organisms and with their environment. Organisational hierarchy:

LevelWhat it includes
OrganismIndividual
PopulationIndividuals of a single species in an area and time
CommunityPopulations of several species in the same area
EcosystemCommunity + interacting abiotic factors
BiomeSet of similar ecosystems at large geographic scale
BiosphereAll life on Earth; the sum of all biomes
Population attributeWhat it describes
Size (N)Total number of individuals
DensityIndividuals per unit area or volume
Spatial distributionClumped (patches) | Uniform | Random
Age structureExpanding pyramid (growing) | Stable | Declining (shrinking)
Demographic variablesΔN = (Birth rate + Immigration) − (Mortality + Emigration)
⚠️ Trap: "A meadow is not a population of grass" → it is a community (grass + insects + birds + microbiota) or an ecosystem if it includes the physical environment. | Confusing "population" with "species" or with "community".
7.1.3–7.1.4 Growth models and regulatory factors
AspectExponential modelLogistic model
ResourcesUnlimitedLimited
Curve shapeJS (sigmoidal)
Is there K?NoYes — population slows as it approaches K
RealismLow; only short-term (invasion, recovery)High; closer to stable natural populations
Growth rateConstant (r)Decreases as it approaches K

K = Carrying capacity: maximum population size the environment can sustain indefinitely (determined by available water, food, and space).

FeatureDensity-dependentDensity-independent
EffectIncreases as density increasesDoes not depend on number of individuals
NatureBiotic (mostly)Abiotic (mostly)
ExamplesCompetition, predation, disease, parasitism, social stressDroughts, floods, fires, hurricanes, frosts
RoleTend to stabilise the population near KCause sudden fluctuations independent of population size
⚠️ Traps: Believing a population can grow exponentially forever → there is always a K. | "All regulation is due to food shortage" → predation, disease, and social stress are also density-dependent.
🧠 Scenario: A fire eliminates 80% of deer. Wolves also decline. What factor affected each? A: Deer: density-independent factor (fire). Wolves: density-dependent factor (prey scarcity).
7.1.5–7.1.6 r and K selection + Human population
Featurer-selectionK-selection
Body sizeSmallLarge
Sexual maturityEarlyLate
OffspringMany, smallFew, large
Parental careMinimal or noneHigh and prolonged
Juvenile mortalityHighLow
Typical environmentUnstable, changing, disturbedStable, near K
Strategy"Bet on quantity""Bet on quality"
ExamplesBacteria, insects, weeds, mice, toadsElephants, whales, humans, trees, condors

Human population: extreme K. Factors that accelerated growth: agriculture, medicine, sanitation, fossil energy → reduced mortality without proportionally reducing birth rate → recent exponential expansion.

  • Demographic transition: pre-industrial (high birth rate + high death rate) → early industrial (high birth rate + low death rate → explosion) → late industrial (low birth rate + low death rate → stabilisation) → post-industrial (possible decline).
  • Ecological impacts: intensive resource consumption, deforestation/urbanisation, pollution, biodiversity loss, modification of biogeochemical cycles.
⚠️ Traps: r and K are extremes of a gradient — most species fall at intermediate points. | Humans are NOT exempt from ecological rules: technology extends K, but planetary resources are finite.
🧠 Scenario: A species produces thousands of eggs, provides no parental care, juveniles mature in weeks and live only months. r or K selection? A: Typical r-selection.
7.2.1–7.2.4 Structure, niche and competition in communities
  • Community = populations of different species in the same area. (Do not confuse with ecosystem, which also includes abiotic factors.)
  • Types of key species: Dominant species = very abundant, controls by biomass. Keystone species = not necessarily abundant, but its effect is disproportionate. Pioneer species = first to colonise disturbed areas.
ConceptWhat it describesAnalogy
HabitatWhere a species lives"Address"
Ecological nicheHow it lives, what it uses, what it tolerates, when it acts, how it interacts"Profession + lifestyle + address"
NicheDefinition
FundamentalWhere the species could live without interactions (theoretical potential)
RealisedWhere it actually lives after competition → always ≤ fundamental
Type of competitionDescriptionPossible outcome
IntraspecificAmong individuals of the same species; most intense at high densityDensity-dependent regulatory factor
InterspecificBetween different species with overlapping nichesCompetitive exclusion or resource partitioning
ExploitationConsume the same resource (no direct contact)Advantage to the more efficient
InterferenceOne directly blocks the other's access (aggression, territoriality)Displacement or forced coexistence

Gause's principle: two species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely → the one that exploits the resource better displaces the other (competitive exclusion). Coexistence requires differences in the niche.

⚠️ Traps: Niche ≠ habitat. | Dominant species ≠ keystone species (a keystone has enormous impact without necessarily being abundant). | Competition is not always physical aggression — it can be "using the resource first".
🧠 Scenario: Two birds in the same tree eat the same seeds, at the same time, on the same branch. What do you predict? A: Intense competition → long-term competitive exclusion or resource partitioning (time, tree height, seed type).
7.2.5–7.2.7 Interactions, structural changes and succession
InteractionEffect on AEffect on BNotationExample
MutualismBenefitBenefit+ / +Pollinator and flower; mycorrhiza
CommensalismBenefitNo effect+ / 0Remora on a shark
PredationBenefit (predator)Harm (death)+ / −Lion and zebra
HerbivoryBenefit (herbivore)Harm (plant)+ / −Cow and grass
ParasitismBenefit (parasite)Harm (no immediate death)+ / −Tick on a dog
CompetitionHarmHarm− / −Two plants competing for light
AmensalismNo effectHarm0 / −Tree whose shade kills plants below

Key difference: Predator usually kills immediately. Parasite typically does not kill immediately (lives at the host's expense for a prolonged period).

FeaturePrimary successionSecondary succession
Initial conditionNo soil (bare rock, lava, retreating glacier)Community existed before; soil is preserved
SpeedVery slow (centuries or millennia)Faster (decades)
Typical pioneersLichens, mosses (no soil needed)Annual herbs, weeds
Typical causeVolcano, glacier, new duneFire, logging, abandoned farmland
  • Trophic cascade effect: changes at one level propagate to others. E.g.: removal of wolves (Yellowstone) → deer increase → overgrazing of willows → fewer beavers → change in waterways.
  • Lichens (fungus + alga/cyanobacterium) are the pioneers of primary succession: dissolve rock with acids, initiate soil formation.
⚠️ Traps: "Primary succession" ≠ "secondary" → the key is soil (secondary preserves it). | Succession does NOT always end in the same climax community (depends on climate, history, random events). | Reducing interactions to "predator and prey" — the exam usually asks for all 5-6 types with sign notation.
🧠 Scenario: Species A benefits; species B is not clearly affected. What interaction is this? A: Commensalism (+ / 0).
7.3.1–7.3.2 Ecosystem dynamics and energy flow
ProcessFeature
Energy flowUnidirectional — degraded as heat at each step; not recycled
Matter / nutrient cycleCyclic — elements are reused between organisms and environment
Trophic levelWhoExample (10,000 kcal base)
1st — ProducersPlants, algae, cyanobacteria (photosynthesis) or bacteria (chemosynthesis)10,000 kcal
2nd — Primary consumersHerbivores (cow, caterpillar)1,000 kcal
3rd — Secondary consumersPrimary carnivores (toad, wolf)100 kcal
4th — Tertiary consumersTop carnivores (eagle, shark)10 kcal

10% rule: only ~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level; ~90% is lost as heat (metabolism, respiration, excretion). This is why energy pyramids always decrease and food chains rarely exceed 4-5 levels.

⚠️ Traps:
• "Energy is recycled like matter" → FALSE. Energy flows unidirectionally and is lost as heat.
• "Photosynthesis is the only energy input" → FALSE. Chemosynthesis provides energy in lightless ecosystems (deep-sea hydrothermal vents).
🧠 Scenario: Why are there fewer eagles than mice in an ecosystem? A: 10% rule. Mice receive ~10% of plant energy; eagles receive only ~10% of that from mice. Less energy is available at higher trophic levels.
7.3.3–7.3.4 Primary productivity and biogeochemical cycles
ConceptWhat it measures
GPP (Gross Primary Productivity)Total energy captured by producers (photosynthesis or chemosynthesis)
Producer respiration (R)Energy producers themselves use to stay alive
NPP = GPP − REnergy stored as new biomass: available to herbivores and the rest of the ecosystem

Productivity by biome: Tropical rainforest >> temperate forest > savanna > taiga > grassland > tundra >> desert

Nitrogen cycle (most frequently examined):

ProcessWhat it doesWho carries it out
FixationAtmospheric N₂ → NH₄⁺ (assimilable form)Rhizobium (legume nodules), cyanobacteria, free-living Azotobacter
NitrificationNH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻Nitrosomonas → Nitrobacter
AssimilationNO₃⁻ or NH₄⁺ → proteins and nucleic acidsPlants (then passes through the food chain)
AmmonificationNitrogenous organic matter → NH₄⁺Decomposers (bacteria and fungi)
DenitrificationNO₃⁻ → N₂ (returns to air)Anaerobic denitrifying bacteria
  • C cycle: photosynthesis (CO₂ → organic) ↔ respiration and decomposition (organic → CO₂). Fossil fuels = carbon stored millions of years ago, massively released by human combustion.
  • P cycle: no significant gaseous phase. Main reservoir: rocks. Released slowly by weathering. Depleted in soils with intensive cultivation → reason for use of phosphate fertilisers.
  • Decomposers are essential in ALL cycles: they release nutrients trapped in dead biomass.
🔬 Process — Carbon cycle (full narrative)
  1. Photosynthesis: plants/algae/cyanobacteria fix atmospheric CO₂ into organic biomass.
  2. Carbon flows through the food chain (herbivores → carnivores).
  3. Cellular respiration (all organisms): organic → CO₂ to air.
  4. Decomposition (fungi + bacteria): dead biomass → CO₂.
  5. Some carbon is trapped for millions of years in fossil fuels (organic matter not decomposed under anaerobic conditions).
  6. Oceans: CO₂ dissolves ↔ bicarbonates (continuous exchange).
  7. Human impact: fossil combustion and deforestation release carbon accumulated over millions of years → CO₂ accumulation → global warming.
⚠️ Traps: GPP ≠ NPP — if asked "energy available for herbivores" = NPP. | Atmospheric nitrogen (78% of air) is inaccessible without nitrogen-fixing bacteria. | The P cycle has no gaseous phase. | Energy flows; matter cycles — they are not the same.
🧠 Scenario: If all decomposers disappear, what happens? A: Nutrients become trapped in dead biomass. Plants cannot access recycled N, P, or C. Productivity collapses within a few years.
7.3.5–7.3.6 Human disturbance and climate change
CycleHuman activityConsequence
CarbonFossil combustion, deforestationCO₂ accumulation → global warming, ocean acidification
NitrogenNitrogen fertilisers, combustion, livestock farmingRunoff → eutrophication, "dead zones"
PhosphorusPhosphate fertilisers, detergentsEutrophication; depletion of mineral reserves
WaterOverexploitation, dams, alteration of waterwaysWater stress, salinisation, wetland loss

Eutrophication (key process for the exam):

🔬 Process — Eutrophication step by step
  1. Excess N and P enter the water body (fertilisers, wastewater).
  2. Algae and cyanobacteria proliferate massively (algal bloom).
  3. The surface layer blocks light → submerged aquatic plants die.
  4. Algae die en masse and sink to the bottom.
  5. Aerobic decomposers consume dissolved O₂ in the water.
  6. Hypoxic or anoxic zone at the bottom → fish and invertebrates die from asphyxia.
  7. Result: "dead zone" (e.g. Gulf of Mexico, Baltic Sea).
Climate change effectEcological consequence
Temperature increaseSpecies shift to higher latitudes/altitudes
Changes in phenologyDesynchronisation between pollinators, prey, and predators
Permafrost thawingRelease of CO₂ and methane (positive feedback) → more warming
Ocean acidificationDissolved CO₂ lowers pH → damage to corals and organisms with calcareous shells
⚠️ Trap: "Climate change is only more heat" → FALSE. It also alters precipitation, cycles, habitat distribution, extreme events, and ocean chemistry. | Studying cycles as "closed" processes without including human impact.
🧠 Scenario: A plant blooms 2 weeks earlier due to warming, but its pollinator does not advance its migration. What do you predict? A: Phenological mismatch → plant not pollinated efficiently → reproduction falls → pollinator loses its resource. Mutualism disruption caused by climate change.
7.4.1–7.4.3 Biosphere, climate and terrestrial biomes

Biosphere: the sum of all Earth's ecosystems. Climate (combination of temperature, precipitation, latitude, altitude, and atmospheric circulation) is the primary determinant of biome distribution.

BiomeClimatePrecipitationDominant vegetationProductivity
Tropical rainforestWarm and humid year-round>200 cm/yearDense stratified trees, epiphytes, lianasVery high
SavannaWarm with a marked dry season50–150 cm/yearTall grasses + scattered treesMedium-high
DesertHot or cold; very dry<25 cm/yearSparse plants, succulents, extensive rootsVery low
Grassland / steppeSeasonal temperate25–75 cm/yearDominant grasses, few treesMedium (high agricultural yield)
Temperate forestTemperate with 4 seasons75–150 cm/yearDeciduous trees (oak, maple, beech)Medium-high
Taiga / boreal forestCold, long wintersLow-moderateConifers (pines, firs)Medium-low
TundraVery cold, permafrostVery lowMosses, lichens, dwarf herbsVery low
  • Tropical rainforest: paradoxically nutrient-poor soil (nutrients are in the living biomass; very rapid recycling). The richness is in the trees, not the soil.
  • Grassland: deep, fertile soils → world's major grain belts (maize, wheat, soy). Natural fires maintain grass dominance.
  • Tundra: permafrost (permanently frozen soil below the surface) prevents deep roots and limits decomposition → stores large amounts of carbon that climate change can release (positive feedback).
⚠️ Traps:
• "Tropical rainforest has rich soils" → FALSE. Nutrients are in the biomass, not the soil (rapidly lost if deforested).
• "A single factor (soil, temperature) determines biome distribution" → FALSE. It is the combination of climatic factors that defines it.
• Memorising biome names without associating them with climate and productivity.
🧠 Scenario: If a savanna receives much higher and more consistent rainfall, toward which biome would it tend to shift? A: Toward a tropical rainforest (high temperature) or temperate forest (lower temperature). Greater humidity allows dense trees and displaces grasses.
7.4.4–7.4.5 Aquatic ecosystems, threats and sustainable development
CategorySubcategoriesKey factorsSpecial note
Fresh waterRivers and streams (lotic)Current, O₂, substrateHighly oxygenated by movement
Lakes and ponds (lentic)Depth, light, stratificationCan stratify thermally
WetlandsWater periodicityHigh productivity and biodiversity
MarineOpen oceanLight, depth, temperaturePhotic zone (0–200m) vs aphotic (>200m)
Coral reefsWarm, clear, shallow waterHighest biodiversity per area in the marine world
Coastal / intertidal zonesTides, variable salinityOrganisms tolerant of desiccation and wave action
EstuariesChanging salinity (river + sea)Very productive; fish nurseries

Photic vs aphotic zone: Photic (~0–200m): light present, photosynthesis, producers. Aphotic (>200m): no light, depends on "marine snow" (organic matter falling from above) or chemosynthesis (deep-sea hydrothermal vents → bacteria using H₂S).

Threat (HIPPO)DescriptionExample
Habitat destructionConversion of natural ecosystems for human useAmazonian deforestation, wetland urbanisation
Invasive speciesDisplace native speciesBullfrog, feral cats and dogs on islands
PollutionHarmful substances in air, water, soilPesticides, heavy metals, microplastics
OverexploitationUse at rates exceeding natural replenishmentOverfishing, illegal hunting, selective logging
Climate changeLong-term alteration of conditionsWarming, ocean acidification

Sustainable development (3 pillars): 1) Environmental: maintain ecosystem integrity. 2) Social: equity and human well-being. 3) Economic: productive systems that do not destroy their ecological base.

  • Biodiversity loss → loss of ecosystem services (pollination, pest control, water purification, soil fertility) and ecological resilience.
⚠️ Trap: "All aquatic ecosystems function the same because they have water" → FALSE. The differences between an estuary and the deep ocean are enormous. | "Sustainable development = using fewer things" → FALSE. It requires integrated ecological, social, and economic planning.
🧠 Scenario: At deep-sea hydrothermal vents no sunlight reaches but there are dense communities. How? A: Chemosynthesis. Bacteria use H₂S as an energy source, forming the base of the food chain. Ecology entirely independent of the sun.
📖 Master Glossary P3 100+ terms · quick search

🔬 Biological diversity — Topic 6

TermOperational definition
Adsorption (viral)First stage of the viral cycle: the virus binds to specific receptors on the host cell.
Alternation of generationsPlant life cycle with two alternating multicellular phases: gametophyte (n) and sporophyte (2n).
AnalogyStructure with similar function but different evolutionary origin.
ArchaeaDomain of prokaryotes without peptidoglycan, with ether-linked membrane lipids.
Ascus / ascosporeSexual structure in ascomycetes; spore produced inside an ascus.
BacteriophageVirus that infects bacteria.
Basidium / basidiosporeSexual structure in basidiomycetes; spore produced on a basidium.
CapsidProtein coat of a virus.
KaryogamyNuclear fusion in fungi, following plasmogamy.
CephalisationConcentration of sensory and nervous structures in the anterior region of the body.
CoelomBody cavity completely surrounded by mesoderm.
CladeGroup that includes a common ancestor and all its descendants (monophyletic).
CnidocyteStinging cell exclusive to cnidarians; contains nematocysts.
ChoanocyteFlagellated collar cell; exclusive to porifera (sponges).
Bacterial conjugationDirect transfer of DNA between bacteria through a sex pilus.
ChordatesPhylum defined by notochord, hollow dorsal nerve cord, pharyngeal slits, post-anal tail, and endostyle.
CuticleImpermeable waxy layer of land plants; reduces water loss.
DeuterostomeAnimal whose blastopore gives rise to the anus; examples: echinoderms and chordates.
Double fertilisationProcess exclusive to angiosperms: one sperm forms zygote (2n), another forms endosperm (3n).
Serial endosymbiosisTheory explaining the origin of mitochondria (from alpha-proteobacteria) and chloroplasts (from cyanobacteria).
EndosporeBacterial resistance structure, capable of surviving extreme conditions.
EndothermyAbility to maintain a high, stable body temperature through internal metabolism.
StomaPlant pore with guard cells that regulates gas exchange.
EukaryaDomain of organisms with a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
PhylogenyEvolutionary history of a group of organisms.
Binary fissionProkaryotic asexual reproduction; division into two identical daughter cells.
GametophyteHaploid (n) phase of the plant cycle; produces gametes by mitosis.
GnathostomesVertebrates with jaws.
Gram-positive / negativeBacterial classification by reaction to Gram staining; reflects differences in cell wall.
Pharyngeal slitsOpenings in the pharynx; diagnostic trait of chordates.
HyphaCellular filament of the fungal body; basic unit.
HomologyStructure with common evolutionary origin, possibly with different function.
Amniotic eggEgg with protective membranes (amnion, chorion, allantois) that allows terrestrial reproduction.
LichenSymbiosis between a fungus and an alga or cyanobacterium.
Lysogenic (cycle)Viral cycle in which the genome integrates as a prophage and the cell survives.
Lytic (cycle)Viral cycle in which the virus actively replicates and lyses the cell.
MesodermMiddle germ layer in triploblasts; origin of muscles, skeleton, blood.
MyceliumMass of hyphae forming the body of the fungus.
MycorrhizaSymbiosis between a fungus and a plant root.
MixotrophOrganism that combines autotrophy and heterotrophy depending on conditions.
NotochordFlexible dorsal support rod in chordates.
Cell wallRigid outer covering; peptidoglycan in bacteria, chitin in fungi, cellulose in plants.
PeptidoglycanPolymer exclusive to the bacterial cell wall.
PlasmogamyCytoplasm fusion in fungi, without immediate nuclear fusion.
PrionMisfolded protein that induces misfolding in other proteins.
ProphageViral genome integrated into the host chromosome during the lysogenic cycle.
ProtostomeAnimal whose blastopore gives rise to the mouth; examples: molluscs, annelids, arthropods.
ChitinPolymer of the fungal cell wall and arthropod exoskeleton.
Binomial systemScientific nomenclature: genus + specific epithet.
SystematicsIntegrated study of diversity and evolutionary relationships.
TaxonAny recognised group in the taxonomic hierarchy.
TetrapodVertebrate with four limbs.
TransductionBacterial genetic transfer mediated by bacteriophages.
TransformationUptake of free DNA from the environment by a bacterium.
ViroidNaked circular RNA, without capsid; infects plants.
VirusAcellular entity with genetic material (DNA or RNA) and protein capsid.

🌿 Ecology — Topic 7

TermOperational definition
Amensalism0/− interaction: one species is unaffected, the other is harmed.
AmmonificationDecomposers convert organic nitrogenous compounds into NH₄⁺.
Assimilation (N)Incorporation of nitrates or ammonium into organic molecules by plants.
BiomeSet of similar ecosystems at large geographic scale.
BiosphereThe sum of all ecosystems on the planet.
Carrying capacity (K)Maximum population size an environment can sustain indefinitely.
Trophic cascadeChain effect where changes at one trophic level propagate to others.
Commensalism+/0 interaction: one species benefits, the other is unaffected.
CommunitySet of populations of different species in an area.
Competition−/− interaction: both species are harmed by use of a shared resource.
Density-dependentRegulatory factor whose effect increases with population density (e.g. disease).
Density-independentFactor that affects the population regardless of its density (e.g. droughts, fires).
Predation+/− interaction: predator benefits, prey is harmed/killed.
DenitrificationBacterial conversion of NO₃⁻ to gaseous N₂ under anaerobic conditions.
EcosystemCommunity + abiotic factors in a place.
Keystone speciesSpecies with disproportionate impact relative to its abundance.
EutrophicationNutrient enrichment → algal bloom → O₂ consumption → dead zone.
PhenologyTiming of cyclic biological events (flowering, migration, reproduction).
Nitrogen fixationConversion of atmospheric N₂ to assimilable forms (NH₃/NH₄⁺) by bacteria.
HabitatPhysical place where a species lives.
Logistic (model)Population growth with carrying capacity; sigmoidal (S) curve.
Mutualism+/+ interaction: both species benefit.
Ecological nicheComplete functional role of a species: resources, conditions, interactions.
Fundamental nicheSet of conditions where the species could theoretically live.
Realised nicheSet of conditions where it actually lives after interactions.
NitrificationBacterial oxidation of NH₄⁺ to NO₂⁻ and then to NO₃⁻.
Parasitism+/− interaction: parasite benefits, host is harmed without immediate death.
PermafrostPermanently frozen soil; stores large amounts of carbon.
PopulationIndividuals of the same species in the same area and time.
Gause's principleTwo species with identical niches cannot coexist indefinitely.
Gross primary productivity (GPP)Total energy captured by producers.
Net primary productivity (NPP)GPP minus producer respiration; energy available to herbivores.
ChemosynthesisSynthesis of organic molecules using chemical energy (not light).
10% rule~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level; ~90% is lost as heat.
K-selectionStrategy: few offspring, high parental care, long life.
r-selectionStrategy: many offspring, little care, short life.
Primary successionCommunity change from substrate with no prior soil.
Secondary successionCommunity change after disturbance that preserves the soil.
TaigaBoreal conifer biome.
TundraVery cold biome with permafrost and low-growing vegetation.
Photic zoneSurface aquatic layer with sufficient light for photosynthesis.

🧪 Hypothetical Cases — Unit 3

31 real exam scenarios · Applied reasoning · Organised by topic · Reveal and self-assess

📊 Self-assessment: Completed: 0/0
🌳 T6.1 — Phylogeny and classification 1 case

1. You have a tree where A and B share a node, and that node then connects to C at an older node. Who is most closely related to whom?

A and B are more closely related to each other than either is to C, because their common ancestor is more recent.
🦠 T6.2 — Domains of life (Bacteria & Archaea) 3 cases

2. You are given a unicellular organism with no nucleus. Cell wall without peptidoglycan, ether-linked lipids, lives at 90°C. Bacterium or Archaea?

Archaea. No peptidoglycan and ether lipids are diagnostic. Bacteria have peptidoglycan and ester lipids.

3. A Gram-positive bacterium loses the ability to synthesise peptidoglycan by mutation. What happens to it?

It becomes osmotically fragile (loses structural support), lyses easily, and stops retaining crystal violet in the stain. This is essentially the mechanism by which penicillin acts (inhibiting peptidoglycan synthesis).

4. An ampicillin-sensitive bacterium is mixed with a resistant bacterium that carries the resistance gene on a plasmid. After some time, the formerly sensitive bacteria are also resistant. What happened?

Conjugation. The plasmid carrying the resistance gene was transferred by direct contact (pili) to the sensitive bacteria. This is why antibiotic resistance spreads so rapidly.
🦠 T6.3 — Virology and infectious agents 2 cases

5. A bacterium with an integrated prophage is exposed to UV radiation. What do you predict?

The prophage may activate, enter the lytic cycle, replicate, and lyse the bacterium. This is the lysogenic → lytic transition induced by stress (UV radiation damages DNA and triggers excision of the prophage).

6. An infectious agent is resistant to treatments that destroy nucleic acids (nucleases) but sensitive to treatments that destroy proteins (proteases). What type is it?

Prion. Its nature is exclusively proteinaceous (misfolded PrP protein). It contains no nucleic acids of its own, which is why nucleases have no effect on it.
🔬 T6.4 — Eukaryotes and endosymbiotic theory 1 case

7. A new organelle is discovered in a protist with a double membrane, its own circular DNA, and 70S ribosomes. What hypothesis arises about its origin?

Endosymbiotic origin, probably from a bacterium. The three lines of evidence (double membrane, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes) are the diagnostic criteria used for mitochondria and chloroplasts.
🌿 T6.5 — Plants 2 cases

8. A plant has a large, green gametophyte and a small sporophyte that grows on the gametophyte and depends on it nutritionally. What group is it?

Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts, hornworts). The dominant phase is the gametophyte; the sporophyte is dependent. In pteridophytes and seed plants this relationship is reversed.

9. If all angiosperms disappeared, what would happen to pollinators?

Massive collapse. Most pollinators (bees, butterflies, hummingbirds, bats) depend on flowers. Gymnosperms (mostly wind-pollinated) cannot sustain these pollinators. The result would be a cascade extinction of these animal groups.
🍄 T6.6 — Fungi 1 case

10. If mycorrhizae completely die off in a forest region, what do you predict?

Reduced phosphorus and water uptake in plants → plant stress → slower growth → changes in plant community composition → cascade effects on herbivores and other trophic levels. The disruption may take years but will be profound.
🦑 T6.7 — Invertebrates 2 cases

11. In an embryo, the blastopore becomes the anus. Which lineage does it belong to?

Deuterostomes. This places it with echinoderms and chordates. In protostomes the opposite is true: blastopore → mouth.

12. You find a bilateral aquatic animal, segmented, with a cylindrical body and bristles on each segment. What phylum is it?

Annelid (probably a polychaete if marine). Key features: segmentation + setae (chaetae). Nematodes are cylindrical but neither segmented nor bristled.
🐟 T6.8 — Chordates 3 cases

13. A swimming larva with a notochord and a post-anal muscular tail becomes a sessile adult lacking those traits. What group is it?

Urochordate (tunicate / ascidian). The larva is unambiguously chordate; the adult attaches to the substrate and loses its notochord and tail. The four chordate features are only visible in the larva.

14. If the amniotic egg had never evolved, which groups would not exist today?

Reptiles, birds, and mammals (all amniotes). Vertebrates would have remained confined to water's edge for reproduction, like modern amphibians.

15. A mammal species loses the ability to maintain a stable body temperature. What consequences do you predict?

Reduced activity in cold climates, greater dependence on the thermal environment (like reptiles), drastic changes in geographic distribution and behaviour. Some existing mammals (sloths, hibernating bears) already show partial versions of this.
📈 T7.1 — Population dynamics 4 cases

16. An invasive species arrives on an island with no predators or competitors. Initially it shows J-shaped growth. After some time, what do you predict?

It will eventually slow down (logistic model) as it hits the carrying capacity K through food depletion, space limitations, or the emergence of density-dependent diseases. It may cause local ecological collapse if it overshoots K.

17. A fire eliminates 80% of a deer population. The following year, the wolves that feed on deer also decline dramatically. What factor affected each?

For the deer: density-independent factor (the fire, unrelated to deer numbers). For the wolves: density-dependent factor (prey scarcity, which does depend on the size of the deer population).

18. A species produces thousands of eggs, provides no parental care, juveniles mature within weeks and live only a few months. What life-history strategy does it show?

r-selection (r strategy): high reproductive rate, little parental investment, short life span, early reproduction. Typical of bony fish, insects, and frogs.

19. Can humans grow indefinitely?

No. Although technology extends K, planetary resources (arable land, fresh water, energy, CO₂ absorption capacity) are finite. There are inescapable thermodynamic and ecological limits.
🌐 T7.2 — Communities and succession 4 cases

20. Two bird species in the same tree eat the same seeds, at the same time, on the same branch. What do you predict in the long run?

Intense competition over an identical niche. In the long run: either one displaces the other (competitive exclusion), or they partition the resource (resource partitioning: one feeds in the canopy, the other below; one by day, the other at dawn; etc.).

21. Two squirrel species share a forest. One feeds on ground seeds, the other on canopy seeds. What evolutionary process enabled this coexistence?

Resource partitioning / possible character displacement, derived from ancestral competition. Each species occupies a slightly different niche, avoiding competitive exclusion.

22. Species A benefits from the presence of species B. Species B is not clearly affected. What type of interspecific relationship is this?

Commensalism (+ / 0). Only one species benefits; the other neither gains nor loses. Example: remoras and sharks.

23. After a fire that devastates a forest but leaves the soil intact, what type of succession follows?

Secondary succession. The intact soil allows faster recovery (years to decades), starting with annual herbs and shrubs. Primary succession begins from bare rock and is much slower.
⚡ T7.3 — Energy flow and biogeochemical cycles 4 cases

24. Why are there fewer eagles than mice in an ecosystem?

Because of the 10% rule. Mice (primary consumers) receive ~10% of plant energy; eagles (carnivores) receive only ~10% of that from the mice. There is simply much less energy available at higher trophic levels.

25. A forest has a GPP of 5,000 g/m²/year and producers respire 2,000 g/m²/year. What is the NPP?

NPP = GPP − Respiration = 5,000 − 2,000 = 3,000 g/m²/year. NPP is the biomass available to herbivores.

26. If all decomposers disappear from an ecosystem, what happens to the biogeochemical cycles?

Nutrients become locked in dead biomass. Plants cannot access recycled N, P, or C. Productivity and biomass collapse within a few years. Matter cycles, but energy can no longer flow without the breakdown of organic matter.

27. A river receives a massive discharge of agricultural fertilizer. What ecological sequence do you predict?

Eutrophication: algal bloom → massive die-off and decomposition → drop in dissolved O₂ (hypoxia) → death of fish and invertebrates → dead zone.
🌍 T7.4 — Biosphere, biomes and sustainability 4 cases

28. A plant species blooms two weeks earlier due to rising temperatures, but its pollinator does not advance its migration. What do you predict?

Phenological mismatch. The plant is not pollinated efficiently → reproduction drops → population may decline. The pollinator loses its resource. This is an example of mutualism disruption caused by climate change.

29. If a savanna receives much higher and more consistent rainfall, toward which biome would it tend to shift?

Toward a tropical rainforest (if temperature is high) or a temperate forest (if lower). Greater moisture supports dense trees and displaces the dominant grasses.

30. No sunlight reaches the deep-sea hydrothermal vents, yet dense communities thrive there. How is this possible?

Chemosynthesis. Bacteria use H₂S (hydrogen sulfide) released by the vents as an energy source, forming the base of the food chain. It is an ecosystem entirely independent of solar energy.

31. A region decides to intensively harvest timber to generate jobs. After 10 years the forests are depleted and the economy collapses. Which dimension(s) of sustainability failed?

All three dimensions. Environmental: deforestation. Economic: a strategy that is not viable long-term. Social: loss of sustainable jobs. Sustainability fails when any dimension is completely sacrificed for the others.

  1. Send the SINPE Móvil transfer to 8713 7782.
  2. Send the receipt to Biomaster.oficial@gmail.com including your BioMaster email and the chosen plan.
  3. We activate your access within 24 h.

The SINPE number is for payments only, not for support.

🌎 Students from across Latin America

BioMaster accepts PayPal payments from any country. You can pay with a credit or debit card (Visa, Mastercard, Amex) even if you don't have a PayPal account.

  1. Register for free and try the platform without a card.
  2. When you are ready, choose your plan in the pricing section and pay with PayPal.
  3. Use the same email registered on BioMaster. We activate your access within 24 h.

✅ PayPal works from Costa Rica, Mexico, Colombia, Peru, Argentina and any country. Visa, Mastercard and Amex accepted.
